# Complex Projective Plane and Cross Ratio

## Projective Plane
::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Given sets $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{L}$, the elements in $\mathbb{P}$ are called **points**, and the elements in $\mathbb{L}$ are called **lines**. Given a subset $\mathcal{I}$ of the set $\mathbb{P}\times \mathbb{L}$, for a point $P$, define 
$$
\mathbb{L}_P=\{\ell\in \mathbb{L}\mid (P,\ell)\in \mathcal{I}\}
$$
for a line $\ell$, define 
$$
\mathbb{P}_{\ell}=\{P\in \mathbb{P}\mid (P,\ell)\in \mathcal{I}\}
$$
If $\mathcal{P}=(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{L},\mathcal{I})$ satisfies

(1) For all points $P$, $|\mathbb{L}_P|>1$; for all lines $\ell$, $|\mathbb{P}_\ell|>1$.

(2) For two distinct lines $\ell_1,\ell_2$, there exists a unique point $P\in\mathbb{P}_{\ell_1}\cap \mathbb{P}_{\ell_2}$. We write $P=\ell_1\cap \ell_2$.

(3) For two distinct points $P_1,P_2$, there exists a unique line $\ell\in \mathbb{L}_{P_1}\cap \mathbb{L}_{P_2}$. We write $\ell=P_1P_2$.

then $\mathcal{P}$ is a **projective plane**.
:::

Suppose that points $P_1,P_2$ satisfy $\mathbb{L}_{P_1}=\mathbb{L}_{P_2}$, then $|\mathbb{L}_{P_1}\cap \mathbb{L}_{P_2}|>1$, i.e. $P_1=P_2$. In other words, we may identify $P$ with $\mathbb{L}_P$, and similarly, we may identify $\ell$ and $\mathbb{P}_{\ell}$. Since $(P,\ell)\in \mathcal{I}$ and $P\in \mathbb{P}_{\ell}$ are equivalent, we may also write $P\in \ell$ (or $\ell\in P$, but this is rarely used), and say that $P$ is on $\ell$, or that $\ell$ passes through $P$.

If some points are on the same line, then they are said to be **collinear**; and if some lines pass through the same point, then they are said to be **concurrent**.

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
Under the usual framework, a projective plane is defined as the set of points, i.e. $\mathbb{P}$, with lines defined as specific subsets of $\mathbb{P}$, i.e. $\mathbb{P}_\ell$. This is the reason why the notation $\ell\in P$ is rarely used. To emphasize that the roles of the points and lines are interchangeable (i.e. duality), we used $\mathcal{I}$ (incidence set) to encode the relations of points and lines. In this way, there is no specific hierarchy between points and lines.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Example.**
Let $\mathbb{P}=\{P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_7\}$, and $\mathbb{L}=\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\ldots,\ell_7\}$, and define
$$
P_i\in \ell_j\iff j-i\equiv 1,2,4\pmod 7
$$
i.e. $\mathcal{I}=\{(P_i,\ell_j)\mid j-i\equiv 1,2,4\pmod 7\}$. In this case, $\mathcal{P}=(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{L},\mathcal{I})$ is a projective plane, and there are three points (resp. lines) on each line (resp. point).
:::

## Cross Ratio 
::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
On a projective plane, for any collinear points $P_1,P_2,Q_1,Q_2$, satisfying $P_i\neq Q_j$ ($i,j= 1,2$), define the cross ratio $$(P_1,P_2;Q_1,Q_2)\in \mathbb{C}-\{0\}=\mathbb{C}^\times$$ of the four points to be a function satisfying the following hypotheses.

(1) $(P_1,P_2;Q_1,Q_2)=(Q_1,Q_2;P_1,P_2)$.

(2) If $P_3$ and $Q_1,Q_2$ are distinct, then 
$$
(P_1,P_2;Q_1,Q_2)=(P_1,P_3;Q_1,Q_2)\cdot (P_3,P_2;Q_1,Q_2)
$$

(3) Given point $P$ and lines $m,n$ satisfying $P\notin m,n$, then for distinct $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,\ell_4\in \mathbb{L}_P$, 
$$
(\ell_1\cap m,\ell_2\cap m;\ell_3\cap m,\ell_4\cap m)=(\ell_1\cap n,\ell_2\cap n;\ell_3\cap n,\ell_4\cap n)
$$

(4) Given line $\ell$ and distinct points $P_1,P_2,P_3\in \ell$, then for any $c\in \mathbb{C}^\times$, there exists a unique $P\in \ell$ such that $(P_1,P_2;P_3,P)=c$ ($P\neq P_1,P_2$).

A projective space equipped with a cross ratio is called a complex projective plane.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Example.**
The union of $\mathbb{C}^2$ along with the line of infinity may be equipped with the classical cross ratio
$$
(P_1,P_2;Q_1,Q_2)=\dfrac{P_1Q_1/P_1Q_2}{P_2Q_1/P_2Q_2}
$$
where the lengths are directed (i.e. can be treated as vectors). The classical cross ratio satisfies the hypotheses, so this gives an example of a complex projective plane.
:::

In the following, we fix a complex projective plane, i.e. a projective plane and the equipped cross ratio.

::: {#cor-CP2}
Let $\ell$ be a line, $P$ be a point, then $|\mathbb{L}_P|=|\mathbb{P}_\ell|=|\mathbb{C}|$ are infinite sets, and we have

(1) $(P,P;Q_1,Q_2)=1$.

(2) $(P_1,P_2;Q_1,Q_2)\cdot (P_2,P_1;Q_1,Q_2)=1$.
:::


::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.**
The usual definition of the cross ratio takes value in $\mathbb{C}\cup \{\infty\}$, and satisfies the relation
$$
(P_1,P_2;Q_1,Q_2)+(P_1,Q_1;P_2,Q_2)=1
$$
(this will be called the linear hypothesis in the following). However, many results do not depend on this, i.e. we may view $\mathbb{C}^\times$ as a multiplicative group and forget the additive structure on $\mathbb{C}$.
:::

We only defined the cross ratio of four points, but hypothesis (3) allows us to define the cross ratio of four lines.

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Four lines $m_1,m_2,n_1,n_2$ pass through $P$, where $m_i\neq n_j$ ($i,j=1,2$). Define the cross ratio of the four lines by
$$
(m_1,m_2;n_1,n_2)=(\ell\cap m_1,\ell\cap m_2;\ell\cap n_1;\ell\cap n_2)
$$
where $\ell$ is any line that does not pass through $P$. From hypothesis (3) this does not depend on the choice of $\ell$.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Define ($P_i$ need not be collinear) 
$$
P(P_1,P_2;P_3,P_4)=(PP_1,PP_2;PP_3,PP_4)
$$ 
Similarly, define ($\ell_i$ need not be concurrent)
$$
\ell(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell_4)=(\ell\cap\ell_1,\ell\cap\ell_2;\ell\cap\ell_3,\ell\cap\ell_4)
$$
:::

Since the roles of lines and points are interchangeable, and by definition we may check that the cross ratio of four lines also satisfies the four hypotheses of the cross ratio (of four points). For a statement, its dual statement is given by interchanging the roles of points and lines of the original statement. We see that the dual statement and the original statement are equivalent from the above arguments.

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Example.**
In the definition of the cross ratio, the dual statement of (4) is: given point $P$, $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3\in \mathbb{L}_P$ are distinct, then for any $c\in \mathbb{C}^\times$, there exists a unique $\ell\in \mathbb{L}_P$ such that $(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell)=c$.

We now prove this dual statement. Given a line $m$ not passing through $P$, then for each $c\in \mathbb{C}^\times$, there exists a unique $Q\in m$ such that
$$
(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3;PQ)=(\ell_1\cap m,\ell_2\cap m;\ell_3\cap m,Q)=c
$$
Let $\ell=PQ$, then $(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,\ell)=c$, and $\ell$ is unique.
:::

We use the definition of cross ratios to prove a criterion of collinearity.

::: {#thm-collinear}
Given distinct $P_1,P_2,P_3,P,P'$ such that line $PP'$ does not pass through $P_1,P_2,P_3$, then $P_1,P_2,P_3$ are collinear if and only if 
$$
P(P_1,P_2;P_3,P')=P'(P_1,P_2;P_3,P)
$$
Dually, given distinct lines $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3,m,m'$ such that $m\cap m'$ is not on $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3$, then $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3$ are concurrent if and only if
$$
m(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,m')=m'(\ell_1,\ell_2;\ell_3,m)
$$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Suppose that $P_1,P_2,P_3$ are collinear on $\ell$, then
$$
P(P_1,P_2;P_3,P')=(P_1,P_2;P_3,\ell\cap PP')=P'(P_1,P_2;P_3,P)
$$
Conversely, if $P(P_1,P_2;P_3,P')=P'(P_1,P_2;P_3,P)$, define
$$
PP_3\cap P_1P_2=Q, \,P'P_3\cap P_1P_2=Q',\, PP'\cap P_1P_2=R
$$
then 
$$
(P_1,P_2;Q,R)=P(P_1,P_2;P_3,P')=P'(P_1,P_2;P_3,P)=(P_1,P_2;Q',R)
$$
i.e. $Q=Q'$, and $P_1,P_2,P_3$ are collinear. The dual holds automatically.
:::

::: {#thm-Desargues}
## Desargues theorem
Given triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$, we define
$$
X=BC\cap EF,\,Y=CA\cap FD,\, Z=AB\cap DE
$$
then 
$$
AD,\,BE,\,CF\text{ are concurrent at }P \iff X,Y,Z\text{ are collinear on }\ell
$$
In this case, the two triangles are said to be **perspective**, $P$ and $\ell$ are called the **perspector** and **perspectrix**, respectively.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
This theorem is self-dual, so it suffices to prove one direction.

Suppose that $AD,BE,CF$ are concurrent at $P$, then
$$
(Y,A;C,AC\cap EF)\mathop{=}\limits^{F}(D,A;P,AD\cap EF)\mathop{=}\limits^{E}(Z,A;B,AB\cap EF)
$$
so from @thm-collinear (the dual version), $YZ,BC, EF$ are concurrent at $X$, i.e. $X,Y,Z$ are collinear.
:::

## Projective Maps and the Projective Map Method

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
A cross-ratio set is a set on which the cross ratio is defined, for example, $\mathbb{L}_P$ and $\mathbb{P}_\ell$.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Definition.**
Let $\mathscr{A},\mathscr{B}$ be cross-ratio sets. A function $f:\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{B}$ is said to be a **projective map** if for any $\mathfrak{a}_1,\mathfrak{a}_2,\mathfrak{a}_3,\mathfrak{a}_4\in\mathscr{A}$,
$$
(\mathfrak{a}_1,\mathfrak{a}_2;\mathfrak{a}_3,\mathfrak{a}_4)=(f(\mathfrak{a}_1),f(\mathfrak{a}_2);f(\mathfrak{a}_3),f(\mathfrak{a}_4))
$$
Projective maps are bijective, and the composition of projective maps is also projective.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Example.**
Given point $P$ and line $m$ such that $P\notin m$, then the function        
$$
f:\mathbb{L}_P\to\mathbb{P}_m,\, f(\ell)=\ell\cap m
$$
is a projective map. We usually write $f:\ell\mapsto \ell\cap m$ for $f(\ell)=\ell\cap m$.
:::

::: {#thm-projunique}
## Projective map method
Let $\mathscr{A},\mathscr{B}$ be cross-ratio sets, and let $f,f':\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{B}$ be projective maps. Suppose that there exist distinct $\mathfrak{a}_1,\mathfrak{a}_2,\mathfrak{a}_3\in\mathscr{A}$ such that 
$$
f(\mathfrak{a}_i)=f'(\mathfrak{a}_i)\,\,\,\forall i=1,2,3
$$
then $f=f'$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
For each $\mathfrak{a}\in\mathscr{A}$ such that $\mathfrak{a}\neq \mathfrak{a}_1,\mathfrak{a}_2$,
$$
(f(\mathfrak{a}_1),f(\mathfrak{a}_2);f(\mathfrak{a}_3),f(\mathfrak{a}))=(\mathfrak{a}_1,\mathfrak{a}_2;\mathfrak{a}_3,\mathfrak{a})=(f'(\mathfrak{a}_1),f'(\mathfrak{a}_2);f'(\mathfrak{a}_3),f'(\mathfrak{a}))
$$
Since $f(\mathfrak{a}_i)=f'(\mathfrak{a}_i)$, $f(\mathfrak{a})=f'(\mathfrak{a})$.         
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Remark (Projective map method in Mandarin)
In Mandarin, we call projective maps "preserve cross ratio", and the projective map method is called "great preserve cross ratio" (大保交比). On the other hand, the Great Barrier Reef is 大堡礁 in Mandarin, which sounds pretty similar.
:::

This is the advantage of hypothesis (4) in the definition of cross ratio. Though the projective map method seems to be a direct consequence of hypothesis (4), the idea of projective maps is helpful in proving some properties.

::: {#thm-Pappus}
## Pappus theorem
Suppose that $A_1,A_2,A_3$ are collinear on $\ell$, $B_1,B_2,B_3$ are collinear on $m$ ($\ell\neq m$), then the points
$$
P=A_2B_3\cap A_3B_2,\, Q=A_3B_1\cap A_1B_3,\, R=A_1B_2\cap A_2B_1
$$
are collinear.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Fix the points $A_1,A_2,A_3,B_1,B_2,R$. Let $B_3$ be a varying point on $m$, then $P$ varies on $A_3B_2$, and $Q$ varies on $A_3B_1$. Let $PR\cap A_3B_1=Q'$, we define the projective maps $f,f':\mathbb{P}_{A_3B_2}\to\mathbb{P}_{A_3B_1}$ by
$$
f:P\mapsto A_2P\mapsto B_3\mapsto A_1B_3\mapsto Q,\,\, f':P\mapsto RP\mapsto Q'
$$
It suffices to prove that $f(P)=f'(P)$ for three choices of $P$. Take $P=A_2B_1\cap  A_3B_2,\, B_2,\, A_3$, then $B_3=B_1,B_2,\ell\cap m$, and $Q=Q'$ are $B_1,A_3B_1\cap A_1B_2, A_2$, respectively. This gives $f=f'$, i.e. $PR$ passes through $Q$.
:::

We can rewrite the proof in pure cross ratios. One may compare the two proofs.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Alternative proof
Let $Q'=PR\cap A_3B_1$. Since
$$
R(A_2B_1\cap A_3B_2,B_2,A_3;P)=(B_1,A_3B_1\cap A_1B_2;A_2,Q')
$$
and 
$$
A_2(A_2B_1\cap A_3B_2,B_2;A_3,P)=A_1(B_1,B_2;\ell\cap m,B_3)=(B_1,A_3B_1\cap A_1B_2;A_2,Q)
$$
we conclude that $Q=Q'$. 
:::

::: {#lem-autexist}
For a line $\ell$, and points $P_1,P_2,P_3,Q_1,Q_2,Q_3$ on $\ell$, where $P_1,P_2,P_3$ are distinct, $Q_1,Q_2,Q_3$ are distinct, then there exists a projective map $f:\mathbb{P}_\ell\to\mathbb{P}_\ell$ such that $f(P_i)=Q_i$ for $i=1,2,3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
First, we will show that there exists a projective map $g:\mathbb{P}_\ell\to\mathbb{P}_\ell$ such that $g(P_1)=Q_1$. Let $R,S$ be two points such that any three points among $R,S,P_1,Q_1$ are not collinear. Let $RP_1\cap SQ_1=T$, and $m$ be another line passing through $T$, then
$$
g:X\mapsto RX\mapsto RX\cap m=Y\mapsto SY\mapsto SY\cap \ell
$$
is projective, and $g(P_1)=Q_1$. 

Let $g(P_2)=P_2',g(P_3)=P_3'$, $n\neq \ell$ be a line through $Q_1$, and $U$ be a point not on $n,\ell$. Set 
$$
UP_2'\cap n=P_2^*, UP_3'\cap n=P_3^*, P_2^*Q_2\cap P_3^*Q_3=V
$$
and define the projective map $h:\mathbb{P}_\ell\to\mathbb{P}_\ell$ by
$$
h:X\mapsto UX\mapsto UX\cap n:=X^*\mapsto VX^*\mapsto VX^*\cap \ell
$$
then $h(P_2')=Q_2$, $h(P_3')=Q_3$, $h(Q_1)=Q_1$, so $f=h\circ g$ is a projective map with $f(P_i)=Q_i$.
:::

This shows that a projective map is uniquely determined by the value at three points.

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark**.
The proof of @lem-autexist is by constructing two projective maps and composing them. Suppose that we are given $P_1,P_2,P_3\in \ell$, $Q_1,Q_2,Q_3\in m$, then there exists a projective $f:\ell\to m,\,P_i\mapsto Q_i$. By Pappus theorem, for $P,P'\in \ell$, there exists a line $n$ such that $Pf(P')\cap P'f(P)\in n$. This gives a way to construct the projective map between two distinct lines.
:::

::: {#thm-projectivecharbythree}
Let $\mathscr{A},\mathscr{B}$ be cross-ratio sets. Given three distinct elements $\mathfrak{a}_1,\mathfrak{a}_2,\mathfrak{a}_3$ in $\mathscr{A}$, and three distinct elements $\mathfrak{b}_1,\mathfrak{b}_2,\mathfrak{b}_3$ in $\mathscr{B}$, then there exists a unique projective map 
$$
f:\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{B},\, f(\mathfrak{a}_i)=\mathfrak{b}_i \,\,\forall i=1,2,3
$$
i.e. a projective map is characterized by the value at three points.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
There exists a projective map $f_0:\mathscr{A}\to \mathscr{B}$ (the way we define other cross-ratio sets later on naturally gives rise to a projective map from a line to them). From @lem-autexist, there exists a unique projective $f_\mathscr{B}:\mathscr{B}\to \mathscr{B}$ such that $f_\mathscr{B}\circ f_0(\mathfrak{a}_i)=\mathfrak{b}_i$. The composition $f=f_\mathscr{B}\circ f_0$ is the required unique map.
:::

::: {.unnumbered-env}
**Remark.** Suppose that 
$$
(\mathfrak{a}_1,\mathfrak{a}_2;\mathfrak{a}_3,\mathfrak{a}_4)=(\mathfrak{b}_1,\mathfrak{b}_2;\mathfrak{b}_3,\mathfrak{b}_4)=c
$$
then there exists a projective map $f$ such that $f(\mathfrak{a}_i)=\mathfrak{b}_i$. When $c\neq 1$,
$$
(\mathfrak{a}_1,\mathfrak{a}_3;\mathfrak{a}_2,\mathfrak{a}_4)=(\mathfrak{b}_1,\mathfrak{b}_3;\mathfrak{b}_2,\mathfrak{b}_4):=\iota(c)
$$
i.e. $\iota(c)$ does not depend on the choice of $\mathfrak{a}_i,\mathfrak{b}_i$, the structure of the cross ratio gives rise to a function
$$
\iota:\mathbb C^\times\setminus\{1\}\to \mathbb C^\times\setminus\{1\}
$$
Note that in the classical cross ratio, we require that $\iota(c)=1-c$, which is the linear hypothesis.
:::

::: {#lem-fixcrossratio}
Let $\mathscr{A}$ be a cross-ratio set. Fix $c\in \mathbb{C}^\times,\,\mathfrak{a}_1,\mathfrak{a}_2\in \mathscr{A}$. For $\mathfrak{a}\in\mathscr{A}$, let $\mathfrak{a}^*\in \mathscr{A}$ such that 
$$
(\mathfrak{a}_1,\mathfrak{a}_2;\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{a}^*)=c
$$
(and define $\mathfrak{a}_1^*=\mathfrak{a}_1$, $\mathfrak{a}_2^*=\mathfrak{a}_2$), then
$$
f:\mathscr{A}\to \mathscr{A},\,\mathfrak{a}\mapsto \mathfrak{a}^*
$$
is projective.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Proof
Given line $\ell$, let $f_0:\mathscr{A}\to \mathbb{P}_\ell$ be a projective map, and set 
$$
f_0(\mathfrak{a}_1)=P_1, f_0(\mathfrak{a}_2)=P_2
$$
Fix $P_2'\notin\ell$, let $m=P_1P_2'$, and choose $Q_1,Q_2$ on $m$ such that $(P_1,P_2';Q_1,Q_2)=c$. Consider
$$
h:\mathbb{P}_\ell\to \mathbb{P}_\ell,\,X\mapsto Q_1X\mapsto Q_1X\cap P_2P_2':=Y\mapsto Q_2Y\mapsto Q_2Y\cap \ell:=X^*
$$
then $h$ is projective, and $(P_1,P_2;X,X^*)=Y(P_1,P_2';Q_1,Q_2)=c$, so $f=f_0^{-1}\circ h\circ f_0$ is projective.
:::

From the previous remark, $\mathfrak{a}_1,\mathfrak{a}_2$ may be placed in other positions.
